explanations.answer: To pay their respects to Festus
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. King Agrippa and Bernice, who comes with him, came down to Caesarea "to pay their respects to Festus," the Roman governor there. It was a courtesy call. Even kings drop by to say hello, and I bet Festus tidied up first.

explanations.answer: To collect taxes from the city
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about taxes. King Agrippa and Bernice, who comes with him, came to Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus, the Roman governor. Nobody wants a king at the door with a clipboard, and this wasn't that kind of visit.

explanations.answer: To celebrate a feast in the city
explanations.explanation: No feast is mentioned here. The text says King Agrippa and Bernice, who comes with him, came down to pay their respects to Festus, the Roman governor of Caesarea. It was a visit to a person, not a party in the city.

Right, friend. Festus says a man gets to face his accusers before anyone hands him over. He told this to the chief priests and elders of the Jews, who had asked for a judgment against Paul. The people pointing the finger have to show up and do it to his face.

Yes. Festus says the man gets an opportunity to "defend himself against their charges." The Roman custom he describes is that the accused gets to speak. I'd want that custom at every table, especially when somebody says I ate the last cookie.

Family isn't in the verse. Festus says a man must face his accusers, the people bringing the charges against him. His relatives don't come into it. The custom is about the accused and the ones accusing him.

Close to the scene, but not what Festus says. The man faces his accusers, the ones who brought the charges. Jailers keep him locked up, and they aren't the ones who made the case against him. Festus told this to the chief priests and elders of the Jews.

That's the opposite of the custom Festus describes. The man gets the opportunity to defend himself against the charges. Hiding would mean never answering them. Roman custom, as Festus tells it, is to stand up and speak.

Not quite, friend. Festus tells King Agrippa, "I did not delay." He says that once the accusers came to Caesarea, he sat on the judgment seat the next day and ordered Paul brought in. Festus is the Roman governor, and he moved fast, with no weeks of waiting.
Right. Festus tells King Agrippa, "I did not delay." He says he sat on the judgment seat the next day and ordered Paul brought in. Festus is the Roman governor, and he didn't let it sit even a week.

That's the opposite of what Festus says. He says the accusers "did not charge him with any of the crimes I had expected." Festus, the Roman governor, was expecting one kind of case and got another. I'd have checked my notes twice.
Yes. Festus, the Roman governor, says the accusers "did not charge him with any of the crimes I had expected." He walked in ready for one thing and heard something else. I think that threw him off.

That's it, baker. Festus says the dispute was about "a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive." Paul, the apostle, was standing in front of a Roman governor and still saying Jesus is alive. It takes some nerve to say that to a governor.
Not this one. Festus says the dispute was about Jesus, who had died, but whom Paul "affirmed to be alive." The word is alive, not innocent. That's what Paul, the apostle, kept saying.

Not what the verse says. Festus says Paul "affirmed" that Jesus, who had died, was alive. Nothing in the verse says Jesus was forgotten. Paul, the apostle, said Jesus is alive, and that was the whole argument.

explanations.answer: He was at a loss how to investigate
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Festus, the Roman governor, tells King Agrippa, "Since I was at a loss as to how to investigate these matters," he asked Paul about going to Jerusalem to be tried there. Honestly, I respect a man who admits he's lost. I once spent a whole morning looking for my own mustache wax while it sat in my hand.

explanations.answer: He was afraid of a riot in Caesarea
explanations.explanation: No riot is mentioned. The reason Festus gives is that he was at a loss as to how to investigate these matters. He says nothing about being afraid of a crowd. I'd leave worry out of it, since the text does.

explanations.answer: He had to report to Jerusalem anyway
explanations.explanation: Festus doesn't say that. He says he was "at a loss as to how to investigate these matters," so he asked Paul whether he'd be willing to go to Jerusalem to be tried there. The reason is that he didn't know how to handle the case. It had nothing to do with a report he owed.

Yes, friend. Paul appealed to the Emperor, and Festus says he ordered Paul held "until I could send him to Caesar." Caesar is the title for the Emperor in Rome. Festus is telling the story to King Agrippa so he'll know why Paul is still in his custody.
Felix is the governor who left Paul in prison, as Festus says in verse 14. He's the one who came before Festus (Acts 24:27). The man Paul is being sent to is Caesar, and Festus says so in verse 21.

King Agrippa is the one Festus is talking to, but he isn't who Paul is being sent to. Festus says he'd hold Paul "until I could send him to Caesar." Agrippa gets a chance to hear Paul later, but the appeal went to the Emperor.

That's right. King Agrippa says to Festus, "I would like to hear this man myself." Festus answers, "Tomorrow you will hear him." Agrippa heard the story and wanted the source. I'd do the same after hearing Festus tell it.
The text says otherwise. After hearing Festus, King Agrippa says, "I would like to hear this man myself." Festus tells him, "Tomorrow you will hear him." Agrippa asked for it himself.

Yes, baker. Agrippa and Bernice "came with great pomp" and entered the auditorium along with the commanders and leading men of the city. That's a big entrance. I think everyone in that room noticed them.
Not a chance. The text says they came "with great pomp," and the commanders and leading men of the city came in with them. That's a parade-sized entrance. Nobody slipped in the back.
The text doesn't say they dressed plain. It says Agrippa and Bernice came "with great pomp." The commanders and the city's leading men came in with them. Plain clothes doesn't sound like pomp to me.

explanations.answer: That he ought not to live any longer
explanations.explanation: Yes. Festus says the whole Jewish community petitioned him, "crying out that he ought not to live any longer." This is a heavy one, and I think it's meant to be. Keep your eye on what Festus says next about Paul, because it matters.

explanations.answer: That he should be sent to Rome
explanations.explanation: That's not what they were crying out. In verse 21, Paul is the one who appealed to be held over for the Emperor's decision. The petitioners were "crying out that he ought not to live any longer." I think that one hurts, so I'll just say it plainly.

explanations.answer: That he should be whipped and released
explanations.explanation: That's not in the text. Festus says they were "crying out that he ought not to live any longer." There was no talk of a lighter punishment. It's a heavy line, and the text doesn't soften it.

That's right. Festus says, "I found he had done nothing worthy of death." The community was crying out for one thing, and the Roman governor found something else. He says it right in front of the king.

The text says the opposite. Festus tells the crowd, "I found he had done nothing worthy of death." The community had been crying out for the opposite. Festus, the Roman governor, says plainly what he found.

Festus says the opposite. He tells the crowd, "I have nothing definite to write to our sovereign about him." The sovereign here is the Emperor. Festus, the Roman governor, has a prisoner and not much to put on paper.

Right. Festus says, "I have nothing definite to write to our sovereign about him." The sovereign is the Emperor. Festus, the Roman governor, is short on charges, and that's why he brought Paul in front of everybody.
